title: Fidget & Regulation Basket
strapline: A grab-basket of chews, squeezes and fidgets — safe outlets for busy hands and mouths that help a body settle to focus.
intent: Children who need to move, chew or squeeze to concentrate get safe, acceptable outlets instead of being asked to 'sit still'.
Children learn that fidgeting can help rather than hinder — and where the tools live when they need one.
Children who mouth objects get a safe chewable rather than a small-parts hazard or a bitten sleeve.
Children start to recognise their own rising tension and reach for a tool before it boils over.
Children build the fine-motor strength and sensory feedback that busy hands are seeking.
implementation: Stock a mix: squeezy stress balls, textured discs, tangles, weighted lap pads, and food-grade silicone chews on wipeable cords.
Keep chewables strictly personal and named — never shared — and follow your setting's hygiene and choking-hazard checks daily.
Place the basket where a child can reach it independently at group time, mealtimes and any sitting-still moment.
Introduce tools as helpers, not toys or rewards: 'this can help your hands while you listen', modelled calmly.
Rotate the contents so novelty doesn't wear off, and retire anything worn, chewed through or grubby at once.
Notice which tool suits which child and steer them towards it, building their self-awareness over time.
key_questions: Which one helps your hands feel calm?
Do you need something to hold while you listen?
Is this a chewing one or a squeezing one?
Where does the basket live when you need it?
Did the squeezy ball help you sit for the story?

impact.text: Children shift and hold their attention at group times, using a fidget to stay regulated.
Children begin to regulate big feelings using strategies that work for them.
Children know their own feelings have names and have at least one thing that helps them calm.
Children reach, grasp, squeeze and manipulate objects, strengthening hands.
Children begin to notice what their body needs and do something about it.

enhancements: A personal 'calm kit' tin for a specific child — their favourite chew, a photo, a squeezy — that travels with them.
A visual card on the basket showing when and how the tools help, so children self-serve.
Home-made additions: rice-filled balloons, laminated texture cards, a knotted-ribbon twiddle band.
Pairing the basket with the calm-down corner so regulation tools and a calm space live together.
A chewable buddy attached to a coat for a child who mouths, so it's always to hand outdoors too.

playing_exploring: Children explore the varied textures, weights and resistances, discovering what their senses crave.
Handling the objects is absorbing in its own right, satisfying a genuine sensory need.
active_learning: Children return to the tool that helps them settle, learning a regulation habit that lasts.
Feeling calmer and more able to join in rewards the child for reaching for a tool.
creating_thinking: Children begin to connect a body feeling with a helpful action — 'I'm fizzy, I'll squeeze this'.
They choose the right tool for how they feel, an early act of self-regulation.
